explanation: Mixed bag. A loose physical theme covers fluids, gases and breathing (water, oxygen, N2, syngas, respirable, pressure, sorption). Unrelated code tokens also fire: HTTP headers ('Accept', 'Content-Type'), streams and pipes (.pipe, stream, InputStream). The strongest hit is a code header key, and a 'bottle water' snippet comes second.

Fires on the second word of hedging or concessive phrases: 'least' in 'at least', 'even' in 'not even' / 'don't even', 'however' used mid-clause, 'rather' in 'or rather', 'all' in 'after all', 'as' in 'be that as'. Also on 'to' in 'in order to'. The phrase context matters: the same words elsewhere are weak.

Fires most on the 'case' keyword that opens a label inside a switch statement. It also fires on class and type names after extends, new or a declaration (Component, Context, TestCase) and on middle subword pieces of foreign proper names (Takuli, Benbihi, Chonburi, Antonin). These are probably two unrelated jobs, so it is a mixture overall.

Fires on the first token of a new sentence or clause, especially after a paragraph break or dash: an opening quote with 'For' / 'But' / 'That', or 'At that' / 'During that' / 'And that'. Demonstrative 'that' and clause-initial words are strongest. Some odd hits also appear on ™ symbols and comment arrows.

Two strands. One is 'of' in 'free of' (above all 'Permission is hereby granted, free of charge') and 'School of'. The other is the class-name part of Android/Java imports and API identifiers (LayoutInflater, AsyncTask, inflate, setResizable, TintColor). A few scattered name pieces also fire.

Fires on a word-initial single letter or short first piece, often K or S (sometimes E or G), when the tokenizer splits off the first letter of a word or name ('k|ailasa', 'K|uala', 'S|uspended', 'K|enny', 's|ipped'). It is strongest when the rest of the word follows as a separate token.

Fires on command-line program names and invocations in shell or terminal contexts: the command at the start of a command line (./, g++, gcc, grails, su, aws, firefox, java -) and words about compilers and CLI tools. Weaker on other tool names in prose.

Fires on calls to action and UI or navigation words: 'If you like/enjoyed this post', 'Click the button to', 'Share', 'Print', 'Download', 'next' (as in nextPage or __next__), 'External links', 'Story continues below'. This is website-boilerplate engagement language, with weaker hits on conversational wording.

Fires on subword continuations in the middle of distinctive words or names (Caucasians, NetBSD, Appellee, Magdalene, Percolation, Arachidonic, mingw) and on some code punctuation such as a quote that opens a string key. There is no clear shared meaning beyond word completion.

Fires on determiners and function words, mainly 'the' (and also 'The', 'a', 'of', 'it', 'there'), after a preposition or at the start of a sentence, especially in news or academic prose. There are a few unrelated hits on digits inside years and numbers (2017, 2006, 25,000).

Fires on technical chemical and biological name pieces: element symbols and chemical groups (C=C, Zn, Te, methyl, isopropyl, carbon), and subword pieces of scientific terms (leucine-rich, globulin, methylation, dentate, Bessel). The context is scientific or technical nomenclature.

Fires on words about concurrency and connections: Thread, processes, Channel, DispatchQueue, deadlocked, coupling, correlations, and also 'thread' meaning a forum thread. A few unrelated hits (#[doc], Stack trace, distracted) are weaker.

Fires on the head word that ends a statistic or noun phrase in expository or scientific prose: '%' after a number, 'risk' in 'increased risk', 'worldwide' after mortality or blindness, plus nouns like skills, resources, study. The common thread is the end of a quantitative or descriptive noun phrase, which is fairly diffuse.

Fires on subword fragments inside rare or foreign words and names: the start or middle of uncommon words (B|ho|jpuri, e|icos|atetraenoic, Qiz|ilbash, Hungarian and Turkish word pieces, chemical prefixes like 17-O). It looks like a generic rare-token or word-piece detector with no consistent meaning.

Fires on function words and common words in informal, first-person narrative or dialogue: storytelling and casual speech, often with profanity or personal anecdotes ('thought for a second', 'piece of shit', 'first time in'). Formal or technical text is weak.

Fires on structural tokens in code and markup, such as the ':' in android:layout_width and other namespace prefixes, indentation before a new statement, and identifier pieces in C struct fields. Some odd prose hits also appear (a list comma, 'threatened').

Fires on a word-initial consonant cluster split off as its own token, above all 'cr' and also 'cl', 'ch', 'te', 'anch' (cr|adles, cr|umpled, cr|ickets, cl|utches, Cr|imian), when the rest of the word follows as a separate piece.

Fires on mid-word subword pieces of technical or scientific terms (thym|id|ilate, de|hydr|atase, nucle|ot|ides, Sac|char|omyces, 'reading' in 'open reading frames') and of other rare words and names. There are also odd code hits ('do' in Ruby blocks, a '/' in an nginx location). Mostly generic subword completion.

Fires in scientific abstracts on discourse and connective tokens at clause boundaries: a comma after an introductory clause, 'Thus', 'Therefore', 'according', 'based', 'caused', 'leads', 'aspects', 'The aim of this study was'. It tracks the rhetorical structure of academic writing.

Fires on mid-word continuation pieces and name parts (Mc|Kin|lay, Sw|iss, Sub|strate, Aub|urn, up|regulated) and on the dash after a news dateline ('(KABC) --'). The hits are miscellaneous, with no clear common meaning.

Fires on miscellaneous subword fragments and identifiers in technical text (Daff|od|ils, osm|droid, N|UL|L, the first digit of a year after 'Copyright', acronym pieces like APC and CDF, 'e.g'). It looks like a generic fragment or rare-token unit with no coherent concept.
